hints: Start by thinking about distance - where is insulin made and where does it act? What does that tell you about endocrine versus local signalling?
Consider what triggers its release and which type of tissue releases it directly without a duct.
Think about how a chemical message can reach all parts of the body at once if there is no nerve connection.
Think about what makes only certain cells respond, and what the result of that response is.
walkthrough:
Hormone Means Chemical Messenger**
Insulin is a hormone, which by definition is a cell-signalling molecule. It is a chemical released by one group of cells that changes the activity of other cells.

Endocrine Means Released Then Carried In Blood**
It is secreted from endocrine cells in the pancreas, the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans, when a stimulus such as raised blood glucose is detected. Endocrine glands have no duct, so the molecule is secreted directly into tissue fluid then into blood plasma.

Target Cells Recognise The Signal**
Blood carries insulin all around the body. Only target cells such as liver and muscle cells have complementary insulin receptors on their cell surface membranes, so only they bind insulin.

Binding Causes A Response**
Binding triggers a specific response in the target, for example insertion of more GLUT channels, increased glucose uptake and respiration, glycogenesis and lipogenesis. That sequence of stimulus, secretion, transport, reception and response is exactly endocrine cell signalling.

Final answer: Insulin is a hormone secreted by endocrine tissue/cells of the pancreas in response to a stimulus (high blood glucose). It travels in blood to target cells, binds to specific receptors and causes a response e.g. increased glucose uptake / glycogenesis.

hints: Look first at the grey meal A glucose curve from 0 to 21 min - what is the starting value and the peak value with units?
Ask yourself which organ detects that rise and will then change its secretion.
Now look at the insulin curve for meal A - when does it peak and how high, and how does its timing follow the glucose peak?
Link high insulin to what happens inside liver and muscle cells that would bring glucose back down to the set point.
walkthrough:
Stimulus - Glucose Rises After High-Carbohydrate Meal**
Meal A is 55% carbohydrate, so digestion and absorption add a lot of glucose to blood. In Fig. 7.1 the meal A glucose curve rises from ~87 to $110 \text{mg }100 \text{cm}^{-3}$ at about 21 min. That rise away from the set point is the stimulus.

Detection And Insulin Secretion**
Beta cells of the pancreas detect high blood glucose and respond by secreting insulin. You can see this as the insulin curve for meal A rising shortly after, to a peak of about $500 \text{pmol dm}^{-3}$.

Effect - Insulin Lowers Glucose**
Insulin binds receptors on liver and muscle cells. It causes more glucose channel proteins (GLUT) to be inserted into the membrane, so glucose uptake increases, and respiration rate increases. It also stimulates glycogenesis, conversion of glucose to glycogen, and lipogenesis to fat.

Negative Feedback Completes The Loop**
Because the effect is opposite to the original change, glucose is removed from blood and mean blood glucose falls back to normal, around 80 $\text{mg }100 \text{cm}^{-3}$ by 60 min. Falling glucose then removes the stimulus for insulin release. That reversal back toward the set point is negative feedback.

Final answer: After meal A, mean blood glucose rises to $110 \text{mg }100 \text{cm}^{-3}$ at ~21 min. Rise detected by pancreas, which secretes more insulin to ~$500 \text{pmol dm}^{-3}$. Insulin increases glucose uptake via more GLUT in membranes / increased respiration and stimulates glycogenesis / lipogenesis, so blood glucose falls back to normal / set point.

hints: Compare meal B composition to meal A - with only 3% carbohydrate and 90% fat, how much new glucose is entering blood from the gut?
Even without eating glucose, body cells keep respiring glucose - what must happen to blood glucose if supply is low but use continues?
When glucose falls below normal, insulin switches off and a second pancreatic hormone switches on - what does it mobilise from stores?
walkthrough:
Almost No Glucose Input**
Meal B provides almost no carbohydrate for digestion, so very little glucose is absorbed into blood. The black curve stays flat around 85-88 $\text{mg }100 \text{cm}^{-3}$ then dips to ~79 by 60 min.

Continuous Removal Lowers Glucose**
All body cells continuously take up glucose for aerobic respiration to make ATP. With removal exceeding input, blood glucose falls slightly below the set point / normal range.

Switch From Insulin To Glucagon**
Low glucose stops insulin secretion and stimulates alpha cells to secrete glucagon. Glucagon causes glycogenolysis, breakdown of liver glycogen to glucose, and gluconeogenesis, formation of glucose from stored protein and fat, which can also be respired directly. That explains the small dip then recovery to ~85 $\text{mg }100 \text{cm}^{-3}$ by 180 min.

Final answer: Little glucose absorbed from low-carbohydrate meal B, while glucose continues to be removed for respiration, so blood glucose falls below set point. Insulin secretion stops and glucagon is secreted, stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis from protein/fat to release glucose / provide alternative respiratory substrate.
